image_description:

   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

I don't doubt that gerrymandering has occurred in my area, and when I become old enough to vote my voting patterns and the voting patterns of those around me may play a role in how the voting districts are drawn.

Thanks to all of the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  "The People or the Boundaries--Who Has the Say?" by Helena of Pewaukee High School in Wisconsin; "Representation Manipulation Visualization" by Brett  and "Gerrymandering: A Political Problem" by Mason, both from Columbia High School in Lake City, Florida; "Divided or United: How Voting District Lines Can Be Drawn in a Fair Way" by Victoria  and "Every Vote Counts - Just Not How You'd Think" by Emily, both of New York; "Meandering Gerrymandering" by MHS 6 Block in Wisconsin and “Gerrymandering for Victory” by Elyas of Valley Stream North High School in New York.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, from the state of origin of the gerrymander, and Greg Yarnall of Morristown, New Jersey, a proud member of NJ's 11th district (no gerrymandering required).

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

The first thing I noticed about this graph is that the highlights of the districts don't always match up with the party affiliation. In the  graph on the left and the graph on the right, there are checkers that are red in blue areas and vice versa. It looks very deliberate and almost manipulative, and it must be to separate the parties and just gain votes. 

I wonder if this is how gerrymandering works. If so, how does it get passed without anyone saying anything? I'm also wondering how complicated it gets when a state does not have a perfect grid. 

This affects me and my community because the government can change the national and state congressional districts, which could change how certain ones vote in an election.

In all of these graphs blue has more votes, but depending on the way they are counting the votes, red often gets the majority. I wonder how this is allowed and how can it be stopped. I also wonder which states this happens in most. I would assume states that can be left and right swinging rather than states that are typically one sided. My state is usually a blue states but it is possible that because of how it is counted this is untrue. I wonder what the distribution is in New Jersey. A catchy headline could be "election stolen" to draw attention to the fact that many elections may be stolen or incorrectly counted.

In the past two days, the New York Times has published front page articles on redistricting in Texas and California.

1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

raw_comment: The first thing I notice about this graph is that there are more voters that are in the blue party than the red party. I also notice that all the blue’s and red’s are organized together and not mixed among the graphs. The first voting district gives an unfair advantage to the blue party, because there is no chance of the red party winning due to how it’s organized. The third district is also unfair because the red party won by a ratio of 2:3, which again is unproportional to their population. I wonder how the voting districts in my state are organized and how it could be affecting each party’s representation. My title for this graph is “The Real Effects of Voting Districts”.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |

| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

raw_comment:
In the population of 25 voters, 60% vote Blue and 40% vote Red. 
Of 3 examples for voter districts, 2 of them stand out as non-representative of the voter population.
The center example has voting districts separated strictly by party; no districts have any party variety. 
The graph on the right shows districts being chosen in a manner that sort of 'hand picks' the Red party to be the majority rule. The Blue to Red ratio of each district fails to represent the ratio of the voter population.
The left example shows each district with a 3:2 Blue to Red ratio, which IS representative of this ratio in the voter population. 

I wonder if there's an accurate way of dividing the voters into districts, with minimal corrupt interference. 
The graph on the right, for example, appears to be the least uniform and most varied, but seems to be divided in a way that intentionally pushes the ball toward the Red party, despite having less voters (this could be Gerrymandering).
But if you apply that logic, how is it possible to divide voters without leaning more toward one party? By this logic, would the other two be just as manipulative?

This relates to my community because the American voting system seems skewed, and muffles the voice of the people who vote. How often do you see a candidate lose popular vote but win the electoral votes (2000 and 2016)? How often is either party accused of Gerrymandering? Very.

The graph shows that voter districts can be divided to help one given party win.

raw_comment: Gerrymandering is an incredibly interesting concept in politics. Manipulating the boundaries of an electoral constituency to favor one party is a practice that has been done since the early 19th century. In this graph, I notice who has the majority (blue) and who is in the minority (red). In an ideal and fair election, the goal would be to have both parties represented in each district. I would interpret the first of the three examples as unfair and unequal, because the blue party is the majority in all 5 districts. The second and third graphs, although not equal, are more fair. Within the five districts, they have both parties represented as a majority which is important. This is important because it allows for a more balanced representation of constituents. In a more personal context, this is important because if I were to vote for red party in the all blue party dominated districts, my vote would get lost and lose its value, as well as my faith in a fair voting system

   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

|---|---|---|

| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

I notice that blue voters have the majority of 60% percent of votes in the graph, while red voters have the minority with 40%. How does this relate to me and my community?

This relates to me and everyone’s community because the way these districts are drawn will affect which party controls our state’s government. We need to find a way to draw these districts where voices of both parties are heard.

Catchy headline: Red or Blue- Which District Are You?

A possible headline for the graph could be: "Electoral College: Making Us Voiceless".

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.

| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |
